routes.description: Establish that naturally developed, reasons-responsive self-control constitutes the freedom relevant to moral agency and can support ordinary desert, responsibility, sanctions, and reactive practices without requiring ultimate self-creation or indeterminism.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects practical control and moral competence to meaningful alternatives, distinguishes ordinary causation from responsibility-undermining interference, and explains why stable responsibility practices and proportionate consequences remain justified under determinism.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control is sufficient to justify compatibilist freedom, ordinary desert, and responsibility practices.

centralBridges.description: Define the relevant freedom through informed, unimpaired, reasons-responsive self-control rather than randomness or ultimate metaphysical authorship.
Explain how learning, reflection, practice, and moral education make agents sufficiently autonomous and accountable despite deterministic causal histories.
Justify proportionate, public, rule-governed sanctions and blame as components of a secure cooperative social order.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish deliberate interpersonal control from impersonal causal determination in assessing whether an agent's control has been displaced.
Account for morally condemnatory reactions as fitting and behavior-guiding responses to serious wrongdoing by competent adults.

routes.description: Establish that reasons-responsive agency does not supply the ultimate control required for basic desert, while showing that protection, deterrence, rehabilitation, moral engagement, and rule enforcement remain available on forward-looking grounds.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it separates practical agency from basic-desert responsibility, shows why neither determinism nor indeterminism supplies ultimate control, and provides non-desert foundations for justified social responses without retaining retribution or desert-dependent anger.

motionBridge.description: Show that natural reasons-responsive control does not justify basic desert and that defensible responsibility practices need not presuppose it.

centralBridges.description: Argue that agents are not ultimate sources of their characters and actions under either deterministic or indeterministic causal conditions.
Show that reasons-responsiveness and compatibilist agent control can matter practically without establishing desert-based blame or punishment.
Ground coercion, deterrence, rehabilitation, and rule enforcement in public safety, future risk, proportionality, and least-restrictive means.
Require an independent role for backward-looking desert beyond what consequentialist institutions and causal responsibility already provide.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Use manipulation and malfunction cases to test whether internal psychological responsiveness is sufficient for responsibility.
Explain how evolved reactive attitudes and responsibility practices can be revised without surrendering their protective or communicative functions.

sections.title: Reasons-Responsive Control and the Ability to Do Otherwise
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether informed, unimpaired responsiveness to reasons constitutes the relevant practical control and meaningful alternative possibilities, or whether those capacities fall short of the freedom needed for desert.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Determinism, and Manipulation
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deterministic histories undermine accountable agency, whether developed self-control supplies adequate sourcehood, and whether manipulation cases reveal a relevant gap between causation and control.

sections.title: Basic Desert and Ordinary Compatibilist Desert
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the central conceptual dispute over whether basic desert is required, whether ordinary conduct-sensitive desert is independently defensible, and whether reasons-responsive agency can bridge the two notions.

sections.title: Punishment, Public Safety, and Institutional Justification
sections.rationale: This issue compares rule-governed punishment and proportional sanctions with quarantine, deterrence, rehabilitation, and least-restrictive protection as foundations for legitimate coercive practices.

sections.title: Reactive Attitudes and Reform of Responsibility Practices
sections.rationale: This issue examines whether moral anger and condemnation are justified or indispensable, and whether evolved practices can instead be revised toward non-desert attitudes while retaining social regulation and moral communication.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Introducing indeterminacy into deliberation does not provide desert-grounding control because the agent still cannot settle which of the supported outcomes occurs.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker distinguishes recent libertarian accounts and evaluates their strategically placed indeterminacy before concluding that agents lack the required control.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the indeterministic half of the ultimate-control challenge and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly develops a central route requirement with a clear control-based objection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is recoverable and expressly limited to indeterminacy-based libertarian accounts and the agent's settlement control.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker presents this as his assessed problem for a specified family of accounts, matching the excerpt's bounded warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unresolved outcome settlement to absent desert-grounding control is clear, though the required control standard remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies strategically placed indeterminacy and its settlement problem, but does not examine a libertarian rival response in detail.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central ultimate-control bridge by addressing why indeterminism does not restore authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: The excerpt develops a direct control objection without engaging a sufficiently developed competing interpretation to test charity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says that even strategically placed deliberative indeterminacy leaves the agent unable to settle which outcome occurs.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Because who agents are and what they do ultimately result from factors beyond their control, basic-desert responsibility is absent under either determinism or indeterminism.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso explicitly identifies himself as the free-will skeptic, contrasts Dennett as the compatibilist, and states the defining thesis of his position.

response.rationale: This constructive statement supplies the con route's overarching sourcehood premise and has no earlier opposing locked move requiring an answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it states the central thesis and directly connects causal sourcehood to basic-desert responsibility.

precisionFindings.rationale: The excerpt clearly defines the disputed responsibility as the particular and pervasive basic-desert sense.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal denial is stronger than the brief sourcehood premise alone establishes, despite the explicit basic-desert limitation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sourcehood premise and basic-desert conclusion are intelligibly connected, but the necessity of ultimate self-sourcehood is not defended here.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universal conclusion rests mainly on an asserted sourcehood principle without representative cases or comparison to rival sufficiency accounts.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The proposition directly states the motion-level con thesis that natural agency cannot ground basic desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: This opening statement presents the speaker's own thesis rather than a developed characterization of an opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines skepticism through factors beyond agents' control and explicitly infers the absence of basic-desert responsibility.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Determinism does not eliminate the responsibility-relevant ability to do otherwise because people remain capable of responding to persuasion, changing their conduct, and developing moral competence.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett affirms the host's formulation and then explains a nonmetaphysical sense of alternatives through behavioral change, legal responsibility, and developing competence.

components.text: Explain how practical changeability gives an agent settlement control over an indeterminately selected outcome.
Show why causal factors beyond the agent's control do not defeat basic-desert sourcehood.

response.rationale: The move shows that determinism permits behavioral change, but neither answers the indeterminacy settlement demand nor bridges practical changeability to ultimate sourcehood or basic desert.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is issue-bearing contrary material, yet the decisive control and sourcehood demands of the earlier moves remain uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Practical change under determinism is clear, but its asserted responsibility relevance depends on an implicit compatibilist scope condition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Observed change supports compatibility with determinism, but categorical language does not itself establish desert-relevant alternatives.

charity.alternative: The skeptical claim concerns ultimate or settlement control, not whether deterministic agents ever change.
charity.decisiveQualification: Behavioral change may be causally determined and therefore does not alone answer the desert-grounding control demand.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility inference is sound for practical change, but the bridge from changeability to responsibility-relevant ability remains material and implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Common observation of people changing supports the modest compatibility claim, while the moral-responsibility extension lacks an independent warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central compatibilist-control bridge by denying that determinism disables practical self-revision.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply shifts to practical changeability and leaves the skeptic's more demanding control qualification materially unaddressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt points to persuasion, changed lives, and people turning over a new leaf as evidence that determinism does not immobilize agents.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Free-will skepticism rejects basic-desert responsibility while preserving causal and attributive responsibility and forward-looking moral engagement grounded in reconciliation, safety, and moral formation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly yields to Gregg, and the uninterrupted first-person explanation states the skeptical position associated with his work.

components.text: Determine whether practical change and moral engagement require basic-desert responsibility rather than merely causal agency.

response.rationale: The move preserves the legitimate practical-agency issue while replacing the demand for desert with reconciliation, safety, and moral formation, explicitly explaining the alternative basis.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: The justified reframe directly preserves responsibility practices while denying that their practical functions require basic desert.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move expressly distinguishes basic desert from other responsibility notions and identifies three forward-looking grounds.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is carefully limited to the availability of specified non-desert justifications rather than their guaranteed superiority.

charity.alternative: Practical changeability may sustain responsibility practices even if ultimate basic desert is unavailable.
charity.decisiveQualification: The preserved practices must be grounded in reconciliation, safety, or moral formation rather than backward-looking desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conceptual separation and forward-looking replacement are explicit, with only the full institutional implementation left outside this span.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Three concrete justificatory functions support the distinction, though their adequacy against all desert-based objections is not demonstrated here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the con motion bridge by separating useful responsibility practices from basic-desert commitments.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accepts the practical-agency insight and carefully separates it from the disputed basic-desert conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly grounds preserved responsibility practices in future reconciliation, future safety, and future moral formation rather than desert.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Basic moral desert is a misleading requirement, while sufficient ordinary moral responsibility can still justify coercion, imprisonment, fines, and reputational consequences for violations.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso directly invites Dan to respond, after which Dennett rejects basic desert and develops the Donald Trump coercion example in his characteristic first person.

components.text: Show that sufficient ordinary responsibility can independently justify coercive responses despite rejecting basic desert.
Explain why ultimate sourcehood is unnecessary for the responsibility sufficient to justify legal coercion.

response.rationale: The move directly rejects basic desert as the required threshold and asserts sufficient ordinary responsibility for coercion, but gives little account of the sufficiency standard.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive desert requirement, yet only partially answers the demand for an independent justification of coercive practices.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary-responsibility conclusion is clear, but the key phrase 'enough moral responsibility' lacks an articulated sufficiency criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical entitlement to imprisonment is asserted from sufficient responsibility without supplying the needed proportionality or institutional warrants.

charity.alternative: Coercion might be justified entirely by safety and prevention without any desert-based responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: Calling an agent sufficiently responsible must add a justification beyond the forward-looking grounds already conceded.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion can follow under a compatibilist sufficiency standard, but that decisive standard and its link to imprisonment remain unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on a vivid individual example and assertion rather than defending why ordinary responsibility independently warrants coercion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con motion bridge by claiming ordinary responsibility suffices for justified coercive practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply presses coercive entitlement but does not fairly resolve the skeptic's independent non-desert justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts denial of basic responsibility with the claim that an agent has enough responsibility to justify state coercion and imprisonment.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Coercion and liberty restriction can be justified through self-defense, public safety, proportionality, and least-restrictive means without invoking free will, retribution, or basic desert.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn answers Dennett's challenge in the first person and develops Caruso's recognizable public-health quarantine model and least-restriction principle.

components.text: Provide a non-desert justification for coercion, liberty restriction, and public protection.
Preserve practical prevention and behavioral influence without inferring desert-grounding freedom.

response.rationale: The public-safety analogy directly supplies alternative grounds for coercion and preserves practical agency, while proportionality and least-restrictive safeguards are only compressed in this excerpt.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly answers the coercion challenge with specified alternative grounds, though the governing safeguards are not fully developed here.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim identifies significant public threat, self-defense, prevention of harm, and the explicit exclusion of free will and retribution.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims that sufficiently threatening conduct can justify restrictions, a conditional force matching its public-safety warrant.

charity.alternative: Ordinary responsibility may help justify coercion and express respect for law.
charity.decisiveQualification: Public safety can authorize proportionate restriction without treating suffering or deprivation as intrinsically deserved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy coherently connects comparable threats to preventive restriction, with a bounded gap concerning differences between quarantine and criminal conduct.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The public-safety and self-defense principles provide concrete support, though the analogy's limits and empirical administration remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central alternative-practices bridge through an express non-desert foundation for state coercion.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response preserves the legitimate coercive function while directly disputing the necessity of desert or retribution.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt analogizes dangerous criminal conduct to quarantine and invokes self-defense and harm prevention without free will, retribution, or basic desert.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Deterministic causation does not eliminate accountable sourcehood because autonomous agents become largely self-made through sustained learning, reflection, practice, exposure to reasons, and moral education.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett directly addresses Gregg by name, diagnoses a confusion between causation and control, and answers the Maya and Marina thought experiment.

components.text: Explain how agents can acquire accountable sourcehood despite causal histories containing factors beyond their control.
Show why developed moral competence supports accountability beyond merely forward-looking engagement.

response.rationale: The reply directly proposes temporally developed self-formation as the answer to sourcehood denial, but does not fully explain why causally inherited learning becomes desert-conferring authorship.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive sourcehood premise with a substantive developmental account, while leaving the ultimate-control objection only partially answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Learning and moral development are concrete, but 'largely self-made' remains partly unstable between causal development and ultimate authorship.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Long development plausibly supports autonomy, but the stronger sourcehood implication needs an explicit qualification about ultimate self-creation.

charity.alternative: Developmental self-control may itself result from inherited and environmental factors outside the agent's ultimate control.
charity.decisiveQualification: A history of learning establishes mature agency more readily than it establishes basic-desert sourcehood.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The developmental pathway to mature self-control is coherent, but the bridge from causal self-development to desert-bearing sourcehood remains material.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The listed processes provide representative support for acquired competence, though no argument shows why they overcome the regress of causal formation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central development bridge by explaining accountability through sustained learning, reflection, and moral education.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response offers a serious developmental alternative but does not resolve the skeptic's decisive ultimate-source qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites twenty years of learning, practice, reflection, reasons, consequences, and moral education as the basis of developed self-control.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: An undamaged, informed, reasons-responsive, and self-controlled person can meaningfully be said to have been able to do otherwise despite deterministic causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Following the question about alternative possibilities, Dennett gives a first-person clarification centered on degrees of freedom, self-control, and reasons-responsive functioning.

components.text: State a responsibility-relevant meaning of being able to do otherwise that does not depend on indeterminate outcome settlement.
Explain why well-functioning reasons-responsive agency can suffice without ultimate sourcehood.

response.rationale: The move directly substitutes an ordinary capacity-based meaning of alternative ability, but largely stipulates rather than defends why that meaning is sufficient for desert.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive control issue with explicit criteria, while only partially answering the skeptic's stronger sufficiency demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The ordinary ability is expressly specified through freedom from restraint, damage, misinformation, and failures of reasons-responsive functioning.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The criteria warrant an ordinary practical ability claim, but categorical sufficiency for responsibility remains somewhat stronger than shown.

charity.alternative: The skeptic can accept ordinary practical ability while denying the settlement or sourcehood control required for basic desert.
charity.decisiveQualification: A functional definition of 'could have done otherwise' does not by itself prove desert sufficiency.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The functional criteria form a coherent compatibilist account, although their normative sufficiency is asserted rather than independently established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete impairment and misinformation contrasts support the functional distinction, but no difficult counterexample is examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central control bridge by defining meaningful alternatives through unimpaired reasons-responsive functioning.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies a legitimate compatibilist definition but leaves the skeptic's distinct basic-desert demand substantially intact.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines ordinary alternative ability through degrees of freedom, self-control, accurate information, reasons, and normal functioning.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Compatibilist agent control and freedom from intentional external manipulation are distinct, and possessing reasons-responsive control leaves open whether basic-desert responsibility is justified.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso announces a return to Dennett's causation-control distinction and develops the two loci of control before stating the unresolved sufficiency challenge.

components.text: Establish that developed reasons-responsive control is sufficient, rather than merely necessary or practically valuable, for desert responsibility.
Show why ordinary functional alternative ability closes the distinct basic-desert sufficiency gap.
Show why practical behavioral change entails desert-grounding control.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the missing sufficiency inference: compatibilist control can be present while arguments about alternatives, consequences, sourcehood, and manipulation remain open.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the unsupported inference and states that basic-desert responsibility remains unsettled despite agent control.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes possessing compatibilist control from proving its sufficiency for desert-based responsibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The asserted force is deliberately limited to an open sufficiency question and is supported by several named lines of challenge.

charity.alternative: Reasons-responsive control may be the ordinary control relevant to mature agency and legal responsibility.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its practical importance does not alone establish the further normative entitlement of basic desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between possession and normative sufficiency is explicit and directly supported by multiple identified challenge families.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several recognized argument types substantiate the open question, though their individual premises are not developed within the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central sufficiency-gap bridge by separating practical agent control from desert-based responsibility.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the compatibilist form of control and targets only the additional desert-sufficiency inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says Dennett's kind of control leaves open desert sufficiency and names alternative-path, consequence, basic, and manipulation arguments.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Deliberate control by other agents differs responsibility-relevantly from impersonal natural causation because social institutions must address planned interpersonal interference that displaces another person's control.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett directly denies the question-begging charge and explains the social significance of control by other agents.

components.text: Explain a responsibility-relevant difference between ordinary causal determination and intentional manipulation by another agent.
Show why impersonal causal history need not displace an agent's control in the way interpersonal interference can.

response.rationale: The move identifies planned interpersonal displacement of control as institutionally distinctive, but does not fully establish why that difference resolves the skeptic's desert-sufficiency concern.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the manipulation distinction substantively, while leaving the basic-desert consequence only partially answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: Deliberate interpersonal interference is clearly identified, although the precise threshold for displacement of control remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The institutional importance of planned interference is adequately supported, with a bounded implicit qualification about degrees of control.

charity.alternative: Manipulated and naturally determined agents may share the same internal reasons-responsive structure.
charity.decisiveQualification: Intentional social interference can independently matter to institutions even if structural similarity remains.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The social-planning distinction coherently explains special institutional concern, though its connection to individual desert remains underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The familiar reality of agents deliberately interfering with others supports the distinction, but hard equivalence cases are not examined.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It reaches the top of the subsidiary manipulation tier by directly distinguishing interpersonal control from natural causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the causal comparison and offers a fair, institutionally relevant distinction rather than denying the similarity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes societies, laws, other agents' plans, and deliberate projects that interfere with another agent's activities and control.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: A forward-looking public-health model can preserve distinctions among intentional, accidental, and habitually negligent conduct by tracking future danger and the protection each case warrants.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso gives the extended answer, identifies his model, and uses three parent cases to explain differing interventions and responsibility concepts.

components.text: Preserve legally relevant distinctions among intentional, accidental, and negligent conduct without relying on desert.
Account for differing forms of agency through their implications for future risk and warranted protection.

response.rationale: The response directly explains how a forward-looking model distinguishes cases by future threat, though it only sketches how culpability categories map onto precise interventions.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive distinction demand with a concrete comparative mechanism based on future danger.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly limits its explanation to the importance of distinctions for future threat and protective response.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conditional claim that different conduct patterns can imply different future threats matches the illustrative comparison.

charity.alternative: Desert-based culpability may explain why intentional and negligent offenders warrant different treatment.
charity.decisiveQualification: A risk-sensitive model can preserve the distinction when the conduct predicts materially different future danger.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from differentiated conduct histories to differentiated future threats and protections is explicit and coherent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mother comparison provides a concrete illustration, but broader reliability of conduct categories as risk predictors is not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central alternative-practices bridge by showing how non-desert institutions retain case-sensitive distinctions.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply takes the distinction seriously and supplies an alternative explanation, though it does not exhaust expressive considerations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt compares two mothers and explains their legally distinct conduct through significantly different future threats to other children.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Determinism and free-will skepticism preserve rational deliberation, persuasion, belief revision, and reasons-responsive action because reasons can remain causally effective.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso labels the objection a recurring misconception and answers it by aligning his view with compatibilists on deliberation and reasons as causes.

components.text: Determine whether skepticism or determinism disables rational deliberation, persuasion, belief revision, or action on reasons.
Separate reasons-responsive functioning from the further claim of desert-grounding alternative ability.
Preserve learning through reasons without conceding ultimate desert-bearing sourcehood.

response.rationale: The reply expressly denies the presumed practical consequence of skepticism: deterministic reasons can change beliefs and actions, so deliberative efficacy does not establish desert freedom.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies and defeats the inference from practical deliberation to the necessity of desert-grounding freedom.

precisionFindings.rationale: The preserved capacities and the causal role of reasons are expressly stated without conflating them with basic desert.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Both parties' agreement and the causal mechanism stated in the excerpt support the compatibility claim at the asserted level.

charity.alternative: Practical deliberative change may be offered as evidence for compatibilist free will rather than as a denial of causal efficacy.
charity.decisiveQualification: The same efficacy is compatible with skepticism and therefore cannot alone establish basic-desert freedom.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility argument is explicit: reasons alter beliefs, beliefs cause actions, and determinism therefore does not threaten deliberation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stated causal pathway and shared premise strongly support compatibility, with only empirical detail about belief revision omitted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level con case by preserving natural control while denying its implication of basic desert.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response grants all of the practical phenomenon and precisely limits what can be inferred from it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that rational deliberation is consistent with determinism and explains that arguments change beliefs which in turn cause actions.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Public and proportionate punishment can sustain respect for law and instantiate a consequentialist notion of desert whose justification does not depend on whether determinism is true.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett receives the floor by name and presents a continuous account of law, punishment, desert, and exceptions for impaired agents.

components.text: Show why public, proportionate punishment remains justified rather than being replaced entirely by nonpunitive preventive restriction.
Explain the institutional value of general law and punishment beyond individualized predictions of danger.
Connect preserved social regulation to a consequentialist conception of desert.

response.rationale: The move gives law maintenance and respect as consequentialist grounds for punishment, but it does not fully compare those benefits with least-restrictive preventive alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the institutional-justification demand directly, while leaving the comparative necessity of punishment only partially answered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The institutional claim is clear, but calling the view 'consequentialist desert' leaves desert partly unstable between entitlement and useful convention.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The value of law supports some sanctions, but describing preservation as obviously sufficient compresses proportionality and alternative comparison.

charity.alternative: Public safety and law maintenance might be achieved through non-desert, least-restrictive measures.
charity.decisiveQualification: Punishment requires comparative justification beyond showing that respected legal order has good consequences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Good consequences can coherently justify legal sanctions, but relabeling the result as desert and establishing punishment's necessity require further bridges.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move asserts the social value of respected laws without representative evidence or comparison to less restrictive enforcement systems.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the central institutions bridge by grounding public punishment in maintenance of a respected legal order.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response offers a serious institutional benefit but omits the skeptic's decisive least-restrictive comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grounds punishment in valuable cultural systems of law and order and in the good consequences of having respected laws.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.proposition: Basic moral desert posits a nonexistent requirement, whereas the desert that matters is the familiar, conduct-sensitive everyday notion and is compatible with deterministic causation.
moves.attributionBasis: Dennett is explicitly invited to reply and contrasts basic moral desert with ordinary practices of deserving outcomes, rewards, and punishment.

components.text: Identify a defensible ordinary notion of desert that survives rejection of basic moral desert.
Explain which nonbasic desert concept reasons-responsive control is alleged to support.
Show that preserved practical agency can coexist with an everyday conduct-sensitive notion of deserving.

response.rationale: The move directly distinguishes basic desert from familiar comparative deserving, but the sports example does not fully justify blame, punishment, or adverse treatment.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the conceptual demand but only partially answers the normative role and scope of ordinary desert.

precisionFindings.rationale: The everyday concept is illustrated, yet its extension from winning contests to moral sanctions remains partly unstable and implicitly qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The example establishes ordinary usage but not the stronger claim that this notion grounds moral blame or coercive consequences.

charity.alternative: The skeptic can accept comparative or attributive deserving while rejecting basic-desert blame and punishment.
charity.decisiveQualification: An everyday sports usage does not show that harmful treatment is justified by an agent's conduct alone.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Rejecting basic desert while retaining comparative desert is consistent, but the inference to morally consequential desert is underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: A single sports-language example supports familiar usage but provides weak support for the disputed moral and institutional extension.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It substantially attacks the central desert-dispensability bridge by proposing a familiar nonbasic role for deserving.

representationalCharity.rationale: The distinction is useful, but the response weakens the skeptic by treating acceptance of ordinary language as acceptance of punitive desert.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt calls basic moral desert empty and contrasts it with the familiar claim that the better-performing team deserves to win.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: Because responsibility practices are socially evolved and historically changeable, society can further reform them by relinquishing harmful notions of just desert and retribution.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage occurs within Caruso's clearly marked response turn and presents his characteristic reformist argument against basic-desert practices.

components.text: Show that familiar desert practices are historically revisable rather than fixed by ordinary usage.
Establish the possibility of preserving social regulation while reforming desert and retributive practices.

response.rationale: The move directly uses prior cultural change to support further reform, though it does not yet demonstrate that eliminating desert concepts will preserve every valued function.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the revisability issue clearly but only partially answers the functional-preservation demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move presents further reform as a hope and identifies specifically the desert and retribution concepts proposed for relinquishment.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical evolution supports the modest possibility of further change, and the speaker explicitly frames the conclusion as hopeful.

charity.alternative: Existing desert practices may encode durable social functions despite being historically evolved.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical change establishes revisability, not that every proposed replacement will preserve those functions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from documented cultural evolution to possible further reform is modest and coherent, with success conditions still open.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The honor-culture comparison supplies a relevant example, though one historical transition cannot establish the effects of the proposed reform.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary reform bridge by arguing that evolved responsibility practices can change further.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly supports reformability while avoiding a categorical claim that successful replacement is guaranteed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites movement from honor cultures to individualistic cultures as evidence that responsibility practices can relinquish desert and retribution.

moves.speaker: Gregg Caruso
moves.proposition: If backward-looking desert performs genuine justificatory work in a punishment theory, that theory is mixed rather than purely consequentialist; if desert performs none, it should be removed.
moves.attributionBasis: Caruso resumes the conceptual challenge in an extended turn, contrasting his forward-looking conversational model with Dennett's retained backward-looking element.

components.text: Specify what independent justificatory work desert performs within an assertedly consequentialist punishment theory.
Explain why ordinary desert must remain if consequentialist reasons already justify the relevant practices.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the dilemma: desert either changes justification, making the theory mixed, or changes nothing and is dispensable.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the disputed inference and states the defeating consequence for both possible roles assigned to desert.

precisionFindings.rationale: The two branches and the contrast between purely consequentialist and mixed justification are explicitly recoverable.

charity.alternative: Desert language might have consequentialist value by stabilizing rules and expectations without adding retributive value.
